pairs.rationale: Both openings name the elder as sender and speak of loving the addressee in truth. Third John names Gaius; Second John names the chosen lady and her children and adds others knowing truth. The recipients are not equated.

Jesus connects remaining in His word with knowing the truth; the letter speaks of truth now abiding in us and being with us forever. Word, truth, the direction of abiding and the future with-us promise remain distinct within this enduring-truth comparison.

Both openings join grace, mercy and peace with God the Father and Jesus Christ. Timothy names Christ Jesus our Lord; Second John says these will be with us, names Jesus Christ the Son of the Father and adds truth and love. The designations and recipient forms remain distinct.

Both describe the elder’s joy over walking in truth and use children language. Second John says some of the lady’s children were found walking in truth; Third John speaks of brothers’ testimony and the writer’s children, without equating the groups.

Both describe loving one another as a message or command received from the beginning. Second John explicitly denies presenting it as new and addresses the lady; First John identifies the beginning-heard message as mutual love without that personal address.

Both explain love through keeping or walking according to God’s commandments. First John explicitly calls this love of God and adds that His commandments are not burdensome; Second John repeats the beginning-heard command and walking in it.

Both warn of many misleading agents gone out into the world and connect antichrist with failure to confess Jesus. Second John says Jesus Christ coming in flesh; First John says having come in flesh and its next unit says not confessing Jesus. The actual forms remain distinct.

Both contrast a work-related benefit with loss. Corinthians says surviving building-work receives wages and burned work brings loss, distinguishing personal salvation; Second John warns readers not to lose what we worked for and to receive full reward. Wages/reward and the building test retain their forms.

Both connect relation to the Son and Father with confession or abiding. First John joins confession of the Son with having the Father and abiding in the beginning-heard word; Second John specifies abiding in Christ’s teaching and having both Father and Son.

Both direct a boundary toward people whose teaching conflicts with received teaching. Romans calls for watching and turning away from divisive teachers; Second John specifies withholding house reception and greeting. Their concrete prohibitions and immediate circumstances remain distinct.

Both warn against sharing in another person’s wrongdoing. Timothy prohibits hasty laying on of hands and sharing others’ sins; Second John says whoever greets the person not bringing this teaching shares his evil works. The different outward actions and sins/works wording remain distinct.

Both closing statements prefer hoped-for face-to-face speech over writing with ink. Second John also names paper and the fullness of our joy; Third John names a reed pen and the hope of seeing the addressee soon. Their materials and added purposes remain distinct.

The closing children of your chosen sister connect with the opening chosen lady and her children. The corresponding chosen and family descriptions frame sender and recipient relations without deciding whether the women are individuals or congregations, or naming an otherwise unnamed sister.
